report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is **not supported for humans**. I found no credible clinical evidence that capsaicin shrinks breast tumors, prevents recurrence, improves survival, or can substitute for established breast-cancer treatment.

**Why the claim may sound plausible:** laboratory research has found that capsaicin can reduce viability, migration, or trigger cell-cycle arrest/apoptosis in breast-cancer *cell lines*. Some mouse work also reports smaller implanted tumors. These are useful early-stage findings, but cells in a dish and animal models do not establish an effective, safe dose or clinical benefit in people.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/  
https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335.pdf

**Human evidence:** Reviews characterize oral capsaicin’s potential role alongside chemotherapy as speculative. The human breast-cancer-related capsaicin research I found concerns treating **neuropathic pain after breast-cancer surgery**, not treating the cancer itself.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/  
https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03794388

**Practical implication:** Eating chili peppers or taking capsaicin supplements should not be viewed as breast-cancer therapy or used in place of oncology care. Capsaicin patches/creams may have an appropriate pain-management role under clinical guidance, but oral products can cause gastrointestinal irritation and may be unsuitable for some people. Discuss any supplement with the oncology team, particularly during chemotherapy or other treatment.  
https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/cayenne
